270555191_5f95a940.text: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) is a shell-like structure that surrounds the dorsal and lateral aspects of the thalamus (Halassa et al., 2019)[2](Pinault, 2004)(Mitrofanis et al., 1993)(Guillery et al., 2002).Comprised entirely of GABAergic neurons, the TRN serves as an important nexus for thalamocortical (TC) and corticothalamic (CT) communication (Mitrofanis et al., 1993)(Houser et al., 1980)(Crick, 1984)(Steriade, 2005)(McCormick et al., 2014).This nucleus receives excitatory input from thalamocortical and corticothalamic axon collaterals, which in turn serve to activate GABAergic inhibitory feedback to many thalamic nuclei.This pattern of connectivity is arranged in a sectorial manner that allows for both modality-specific and network-wide interactions (Fig. 1)

270555191_fc6c9672.text: .Feedback projections from visual TRN to dLGN began to innervate dLGN as early as postnatal day 2 with weak inhibitory responses emerging during week 1. During week 2–4, inhibitory responses continued to grow larger, showing synaptic depression during repetitive stimulation. During this time TRN inhibition started to suppress TC spiking, having its greatest impact by week 4–6

270555191_79dca22b.text: .Using a mutant mouse that lacks retinofugal projections revealed that the absence of retinal input led to an acceleration of TRN innervation of dLGN but had little impact on the development of feedforward projections from dLGN to TRN.
